definition: Schema-agnostic databases or vocabulary-independent databases aim at supporting users to be abstracted from the representation of the data, supporting the automatic semantic matching between queries and databases.
details: Schema-agnosticism is the property of a database of mapping a query issued with the user terminology and structure, automatically mapping it to the dataset vocabulary. The increase in the size and in the semantic heterogeneity of database schemas bring new requirements for users querying and searching structured data. At this scale it can become unfeasible for data consumers to be familiar with the representation of the data in order to query it. At the center of this discussion is the semantic gap between users and databases, which becomes more central as the scale and complexity of the data grows.

explainer.lead: Schema-agnostic databases let users query data without knowing its underlying representation, automatically matching queries to the dataset vocabulary. It matters as schemas grow large and semantically heterogeneous, making it unfeasible for consumers to learn them.

tiers.eli5: It's like asking a librarian for a book in your own words and having them find it, even though the shelves use a different labelling system.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on semantic matching between query terms and stored vocabulary so users can search structured data without schema knowledge; a pitfall is mismatched or ambiguous mappings returning wrong results silently.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, it is the property of mapping a query issued in user terminology and structure onto the dataset vocabulary automatically. Limits: mapping quality depends on semantic matching, and heterogeneous schemas at scale make errors hard to detect.

explainer.example: A user queries 'author' while the database stores 'creator', and the mapping resolves the term automatically.
